motivation: Net Flow Rate is defined as Inflow minus Outflow: dV/dt = Qin - Qout. An increase in inflow rate directly causes an increase in net flow rate, by definition. This is conservation of mass applied to the tank.
Since Net Flow = Inflow - Outflow, an increase in outflow rate directly causes a decrease in net flow rate. This follows from conservation of mass: water leaving reduces the net accumulation.

This is a fundamental stock-flow relationship. The water level (stock) integrates the net flow rate over time: h(t) = h(0) + ∫(net flow)/A dt, where A is tank cross-sectional area. Positive net flow causes water level to rise.

According to hydrostatics, the pressure at a depth h below the water surface is P = ρgh (Pascal's Law). An increase in water level (h) directly causes an increase in outlet pressure, assuming the outlet is at the bottom of the tank.

According to Torricelli's theorem and fluid dynamics, flow rate through an orifice increases with driving pressure: Q = Cd*A*√(2P/ρ). Higher pressure causes faster outflow. This is derived from Bernoulli's principle.

The valve opening controls the effective flow area. A more open valve allows more water to flow through: Q = Cd*A_valve*√(2ΔP/ρ). Increasing valve opening increases the effective area, directly causing higher outflow rate.
